comparison: Both evaluate retrograde tracing experiments establishing EN as a significant vCA1 afferent (C28-C35, C47, C118). OpenEval emphasizes quantitative normalization and spatial distribution analysis. Peer reviewers affirm the anatomical connectivity with praise for 'sophisticated intersectional viral tracing techniques' and 'convincing' evidence. Both rate as SUPPORTED.

Both evaluate dual retrograde tracing and intersectional labeling showing vCA1 as main limbic target (C36-C48). OpenEval highlights ~30% double-labeling and projection density comparisons. Peer reviewers acknowledge connectivity patterns without concerns, noting 'EN sends robust projections to the vCA1 that collateralise to the prefrontal cortex, lateral entorhinal cortex and piriform cortex.' Both rate as SUPPORTED.

Both evaluate layer-specific targeting and optogenetic mapping (C49-C51, C58, C121). OpenEval notes unexpected connectivity patterns contradicting initial expectations. Peer reviewers accept findings as part of 'careful anatomical circuit characterization,' noting 'EN projection neurons terminate in the stratum lacunosum-moleculare (SLM) layer.' Both rate as SUPPORTED.

Both evaluate feedforward inhibition via EN→GABAergic connectivity (C67-C72, C119). OpenEval emphasizes converging anatomical (rabies tracing C54-C57) and functional (electrophysiology) evidence with pharmacological validation. Peer reviewers explicitly affirm findings, noting 'EN neurons target inhibitory interneurons providing a mechanism for feedforward inhibition' and 'careful electrophysiological circuit characterization.' Both rate as SUPPORTED.

Both evaluate monosynaptic rabies tracing showing piriform cortex as highest presynaptic source (C73-C76, C102). OpenEval notes quantification directly supports conclusions. Peer reviewers accept findings without critique, noting 'vCA1 projecting EN neurons receive afferent input from piriform cortex, and from within EN.' Both rate as SUPPORTED with perfect claim overlap.

Both evaluate fiber photometry showing ENvCA1-proj. neurons active during novel exploration (C77-C88, C108). OpenEval emphasizes spatial correlation quantification and session-dependent differences (discrimination vs. sociability). Peer reviewers affirm findings, noting neurons 'are most active when mice explore novel objects or conspecifics' and accepting the 'neural mechanism that suppresses the processing of familiar stimuli.' Both rate as SUPPORTED.

Both evaluate chemogenetic inhibition showing selective impairment in discrimination (C89-C95, C99-C101, C107). OpenEval highlights within-subject design and lack of effects on pretest/sociability, anxiety, or fear memory. Peer reviewers explicitly support findings, noting 'pathway-specific chemogenetic inhibition led to an impairment in the ability to discriminate between novel vs. familiar objects and conspecifics.' Both rate as SUPPORTED.

Partial overlap on control experiments (C97-C98). OpenEval R7 includes these as part of broader chemogenetic inhibition evaluation. Peer R8 specifically evaluates control experiments establishing specificity, noting approvingly 'the authors conducted behavioural analysis of locomotor activity, anxiety and fear memory.' Both support the specificity claims.

Both evaluate the integrated mechanistic model (C7-C8, C109-C111, C130). OpenEval rates as SUPPORTED, noting it's an interpretive synthesis well-supported by convergent evidence from multiple approaches. Peer reviewers accept the mechanism, with editor stating study 'suggesting a neural mechanism that suppresses the processing of familiar stimuli' and reviewer noting 'conclusions of the paper are supported by the data presented.' Both rate as SUPPORTED.

Both evaluate anatomical explanation for unexpected connectivity patterns (C123-C125). OpenEval notes explanation supported by citations and consistent with observed data. Peer reviewers implicitly accept by praising 'multilevel analysis approach' and noting study provides 'valuable insights' without raising concerns about chandelier cell hypothesis. Both rate as SUPPORTED, though OpenEval R10 also includes C117.

OpenEval R11 evaluates interpretation of dissociation between activity correlation and behavioral necessity (C112-C113) as UNCERTAIN, noting the 'represent' without 'driving' claim is speculative and differentiation from CLA lacks direct comparative data. No corresponding peer review evaluation found addressing these specific interpretive claims.

Both evaluate speculative mechanistic scenarios (C126-C129). OpenEval rates as UNCERTAIN, noting these are plausible hypotheses supported by citations but not directly tested and require future validation. Peer reviewers rate as SUPPORTED without challenging the speculative interpretations, with one stating 'conclusions of the paper are supported by the data presented.' Divergence in evaluation: OpenEval more cautious about untested hypotheses.

Partial overlap on discussion claims. OpenEval R13 evaluates C131-C133 as SUPPORTED, noting C133 links lack of innate behavior effects to sparse projections with citation support, while C132 is more speculative. Peer R12 evaluates broader set (C126-C133) as SUPPORTED without distinguishing between more/less speculative components.

Minimal overlap (C117 only). OpenEval R14 evaluates historical context claims (C114-C117) about why EN→vCA1 was underappreciated, rating as SUPPORTED. Peer R10 includes C117 as part of broader anatomical explanation evaluation. Both accept the claims but focus on different aspects.

Both evaluate translational/clinical implications (C134-C135). OpenEval rates as UNCERTAIN, noting these are speculative extensions requiring validation in disease models or human studies despite citation support. Peer reviewers rate as SUPPORTED without critique, implicitly accepting potential relevance by noting work 'will be of broad interest to researchers studying the neural circuitry of behavior.' Divergence in evaluation of speculative translational claims.

Both evaluate background/rationale claims (C1-C2, C9-C21). OpenEval notes these appropriately frame knowledge gap with extensive citations but represent prior knowledge rather than new findings. Peer reviewers accept framing without critique, affirming 'The anatomical connectivity of the claustrum and the role of its output projections has, thus far, not been studied in detail.' Both rate as SUPPORTED.

Minimal overlap (C63-C64). OpenEval R9 evaluates electrophysiology comparing EPSC amplitudes across cell types as SUPPORTED, noting finding is somewhat surprising given differential connectivity patterns. Peer R4 includes these claims as part of broader feedforward inhibition evaluation without specific comment on the EPSC amplitude comparison.
